#5451. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5450. Democrats press White House on prediction market betting by staff

Two Democratic senators are pressing the White House to disclose whether employees have used inside information to trade on prediction market platforms. Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) and Jeff Merkley (D-OR) sent a letter to White House counsel Will Scharf on Monday asking what safeguards the administration has in place to prevent staff from using confidential government information to profit from bets.

The request follows a July report that Gabriel Perez, President Donald Trump’s longtime teleprompter operator, allegedly made over $100,000 on prediction market Kalshi by betting on which words Trump would use in more than a dozen speeches. Perez later reached a settlement with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission that required him to surrender his profits, pay a penalty, and agree to a three-year trading ban.

“It has been four months since this White House insider trading scandal came to light, and we write to you to understand what further steps—if any—your office is taking to prevent abuses of power,” read a copy of the letter shared with Fortune.

The letter also asked whether White House staff receive training on rules against using nonpublic information to trade or bet and whether officials contacted the CFTC or Justice Department about Perez’s case. They requested a copy of a memo warning staff against such bets and answers to their questions by Nov. 23.

The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

The case is one of several that have raised concerns about insiders using nonpublic information to profit on prediction markets. In April, federal prosecutors charged a U.S. soldier with using classified information to make more than $400,000 on Polymarket bets tied to the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. In February, six newly created Polymarket accounts drew scrutiny after earning roughly $1 million in combined profits betting the U.S. would strike Iran before the month ended.

The letter offers a preview of the scrutiny the Trump administration could face when Democrats retake control of Congress in January. Warren is expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee, giving her a powerful platform to investigate financial firms and potential conflicts involving the president’s family businesses.

Other Democrats are also pushing for restrictions on prediction markets. On Tuesday, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) called on Congress to ban sports prediction markets, describing them as “sports betting disguised as financial trading.”

The Trump family has expanded its ties to the prediction market industry during Trump’s second term. Donald Trump Jr. advises both Kalshi and Polymarket, and 1789 Capital, the venture firm where he is a partner, has invested in Polymarket. Trump Media, the company behind Truth Social in which the president holds a stake through a trust, announced plans in October 2025 for a prediction market service called Truth Predict with crypto exchange Crypto.com. It later scaled back the initial offering to a marketing partnership.

#5449. Elon Musk wants to build AI satellite factories on the moon—and now SpaceX will compete for NASA’s $10 billion in contracts to build a lunar base

Before going public at a record $1.77 trillion, SpaceX detailed plans in its S-1 of building a lunar economy by setting up factories on the moon to make AI satellites. For Musk’s vision to turn into reality, someone needs to figure out how to transport equipment to the moon, generate electricity there, and keep communication lines connected to Earth.

NASA is putting money on the table to do it at scale. The federal space agency announced on Nov. 7 it selected eight companies including SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Lockheed Martin Space to compete for contracts worth up to $10 billion to transport equipment and infrastructure to the moon. It’s part of NASA’s goal of building a permanent lunar outpost for astronauts to inhabit.

“We are building the Moon Base mission by mission,” NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said in the announcement. “When our astronauts return to the Moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them on the surface.”

The billions in potential contracts show how intertwined the ambitions of federal space programs and the private space sector have become even as they embrace distinct goals, with NASA focused on establishing a place where astronauts can live and work, and SpaceX eyeing lunar space for manufacturing.

NASA declined to comment, and SpaceX did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

NASA wants to carve out its first permanent outpost on the moon, starting with its first phase of robotic explorations of its south pole to identify promising locations for future infrastructure in 2029, according to its Moon Base website.

Then, between 2029 and 2032, NASA plans to build up power systems, cargo transportation, and communications networks to “support long-term operations” on the moon. After 2032, the agency will focus on making the outpost livable for astronauts so they can do more ambitious research and do “future journeys deeper into the solar system.”

The challenge of getting equipment and supplies up there is why NASA is enlisting outside help. It said the eight companies selected under the Commercial Lunar Payload Services program will be eligible to compete for lunar delivery missions over the next decade, building and operating landers to carry scientific instruments, technology, and other infrastructure.

This is on top of NASA’s existing lunar-related contracting program. NASA said it awarded Blue Origin, Impulse Space, and Arrow Science and Technology a combined $1.3 billion for separate mission tasks. Those tasks include verifying communications systems between the moon and Earth, finding ways to move cargo between the two, and sending drones to survey the lunar surface before astronauts get there.

NASA is also trying to solve the problems of generating electricity and maintaining communication lines. It picked SpaceX to launch satellites aboard a Starship to space in 2028 to test the technology that’ll help astronauts and mission controllers stay connected. The agency also awarded several companies (including the Blue Origin owned Honeybee Robotics) to work on power generation and wireless power transfer for a planned Mini-Communications and Solar Tower (miniCAST).

But for SpaceX, these contracts could eventually pave the way for space operations that go beyond shipping astronauts and cargo onto the moon. In its S-1, the company said it intends to build factories on the moon that would use moon-extracted raw materials to manufacture AI satellites, while shipping chips from Earth.

SpaceX said using those lunar materials and taking advantage of the moon’s weaker gravity could “significantly reduce costs and terrestrial resource constraints.” SpaceX also envisions a “lunar mass driver,” which would use “electromagnetic acceleration” to propel satellites without rockets. SpaceX also sees a business opportunity in mining and exporting lunar minerals, estimating the moon has more than 1 million tons of “rare materials” that could go into quantum computing systems and nuclear energy.

But the company’s main goal appears to be setting up a constellation of satellites capable of performing AI computing in space, potentially allowing the company to expand its computing capacity without relying on power-intensive and controversial data centers on Earth.

“This roadmap positions the Moon not only as a potential gateway to Mars and space exploration, but as the first space-based industrial economy at scale,” the S-1 said. “Over time, this infrastructure has the potential to position the Moon as a strategic industrial and transportation node.”

#5448. Agility Robotics co-founder on its Nasdaq debut, lessons from Amazon, and the future of work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 5, 2026 at 6:51 pmNovember 5, 2026 at 6:51 pm

Agility Robotics of Salem, Ore., made its Nasdaq debut Thursday as the first publicly traded U.S. company devoted solely to humanoid robots — offering an ambitious vision for how the technology will change work, and a cautious view of how long it will take.

“Maybe we’ll never have faster-than-light travel. Maybe we’ll never have transporters from Star Trek,” said Jonathan Hurst, the company’s co-founder and chief robot officer. “But we absolutely will have machines that can do all of the physical work that a person can do.”

However, he cautioned, “It’s not going to be next year or five years from now. It’s really a grand challenge.”

Agility went public through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, led by financier Michael Klein. The deal valued Agility at $2.5 billion before the new investment and brought in about $465 million in gross proceeds. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT.

After initially dipping below its opening price, the stock closed Thursday at $11.51, up 2.2%, bucking the trend on a day when the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, its worst day in 18 months.

Agility’s robot: The company’s main character is Digit, a two-legged robot with two arms mounted near the top of its torso that let it lift bins high and recover from falls. It moves totes and containers in warehouses and factories.

Digit 5, the latest version, was unveiled in September. Standing 5-foot-11 and weighing 284 pounds, it’s covered in sensors, with cameras and antennas in its head and safety-rated sensors in protective housings around its body. Agility says it can lift 50 pounds, reach 7.2 feet high and work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day.

But the big advance is that Digit 5 was designed to work alongside people without a barrier. Earlier versions had to be fenced off from workers, which limited where customers could use them.

Agility learned how much that mattered at Amazon, an early investor in the company, which tested prior versions of Digit for moving and stacking bins in its warehouses.

Digit did useful work in tests there, Hurst said, but when Agility asked about scaling up, Amazon said it couldn’t deploy the robots. It showed Agility what it had taken to get its own wheeled robot through three to four years of safety certification, and said it didn’t know how a balancing robot would ever get there.

“The safety case to do this is unbelievably hard,” Hurst said. “Nobody has ever deployed a dynamically stable balancing machine, and it brings new risks.”

Getting a robot out from behind the barrier took years of engineering and standards work. Agility has been co-authoring ISO safety standards for the category and making its case to insurance companies and warehouse operators who want proof in numbers before putting a balancing machine next to a person.

Digit 5 uses AI and multiple sensors to watch for nearby people. Depending on the situation, it steers around them, stops or sits down. Visual and audio cues signal what it’s about to do, and a safety controller triggers its responses when someone gets too close.

Hurst credits the lessons from Amazon, along with ones from GXO, Toyota and Schaeffler, with shaping the design of Digit 5.

“Amazon was a huge, huge part of getting us to that point,” he said.

Amazon made an initial deposit in 2024 toward a $1.05 million purchase of five robots, according to Agility’s filings. Agility recorded about $1.04 million in net sales from Amazon in 2025, 58% of its total for the year. Hurst said he couldn’t speak to whether Amazon is a customer now.

With the safety improvements and other advancements, Hurst called Digit 5 “the scaling moment” for Agility. “That is the unlock,” he said.

One customer, which Agility has not named, has committed to a $300 million, three-year contract for 1,000 Digit 5 robots, according to its filings. The robots would be rented rather than sold, the commitment is subject to milestones and specifications, and the customer gets warrants that vest as the robots are deployed.

Agility has built about 10 Digit 5 robots, Hurst said, with the first prototypes just coming off the line. Its factory in Salem was built to eventually produce as many as 10,000 robots a year.

Financial picture: Agility’s business is still small, with revenue of $1.78 million last year and about $174,000 in the first six months of this year. It lost $362 million in the first half, up from $71.8 million a year earlier. Stock-based compensation, an accounting charge for employee equity awards, rose by about $252 million over the same period.

Agility had $14.7 million in cash at the end of June, before the deal closed, and management said in its interim financial statements that there was substantial doubt about the company’s ability to keep operating.

Hurst called the public markets his biggest unknown.

“I’m completely confident in our market path, our technological path,” he said. If public shareholders agree, he said, Agility will be able to “continue on this mission successfully and raise money when we need to.” If they doubt the company, “that’s going to make our life a lot harder.”

What Agility has that most rivals don’t is robots doing commercial work. As of May, its Digit 4 model had logged more than 65,000 hours across nine committed customer deployments, according to its filings. Digit 4 robots have moved more than 100,000 totes since June 2024 at a Georgia facility run by the logistics company GXO.

Investors have put far higher values on rivals still working largely in pilots, including Figure AI at a reported $39 billion, more than 15 times Agility’s valuation in the merger.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, in a statement. Going public, she said, gives the company more resources to put Digit into more workplaces.

Johnson became CEO in March 2024, when Hurst moved from CTO to chief robot officer. She previously ran Magic Leap, and before that spent six years as a Microsoft executive, leading business development and dealmaking under CEO Satya Nadella.

In an interview with GeekWire earlier in the week, Hurst took the long view on the stock listing, calling it a milestone on a much longer path. Treating a listing day as the achievement, he said, is a finance person’s frame: “I just don’t live in that world.”

From CMU to OSU: Hurst has been on that path for almost three decades.

He built his first walking robot in 1997, as a freshman at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. He stayed at Carnegie Mellon for a Ph.D. in robotics, finishing in 2008, when fewer than 100 people in the world had earned one, he said.

That year he joined Oregon State University in Corvallis, planning from the start to eventually spin a company out of his research. In his Oregon State lab, Hurst’s team built ATRIAS, a two-legged robot that didn’t look like any animal because it was based on a mathematical model of walking and running. It was the first machine to reproduce the dynamics of human walking.

He started Agility in 2015 with Damion Shelton, a Carnegie Mellon classmate who was CEO until 2024, and Mikhail Jones, one of his Oregon State students, out of his lab there.

Being in Oregon helped from the start, Hurst said. Agility was almost alone in trying to build humanoid robots, and the engineers who moved to Oregon to join it were committed to that mission. The company had almost no turnover, unlike the Silicon Valley pattern of people jumping to a new job every six months.

But as it passed 400 employees, it needed experienced engineering managers, and Oregon had no robotics industry large enough to have produced them. Agility had been hiring those people in California and flying them north, so it opened an office there. Today Agility has offices in Pittsburgh and Fremont, Calif., in addition to Oregon.

Impact on jobs: For the time being, Agility pitches Digit as a way to fill jobs that are difficult to staff. Johnson told TechCrunch this week that the company has focused on “manual, very repetitive jobs, that it’s hard to find humans to do.”

Hurst calls the first commercial uses of the technology “step one” toward what he describes as the dream: “robots as part of everyday human life, doing the things people would rather not do.”

Asked what happens to the people whose work the robots replace, Hurst pointed to farming as an example of automation improving people’s lives.

“Early in American history, 90% of Americans worked in agriculture, and today 2% do,” he said. “And the only reason that’s true is because of automation.”

#5447. From House charges to a Senate verdict: 10 parts of U.S. impeachment

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Learn how impeachment works in the U.S., from House charges and articles of impeachment to the Senate trial, the two-thirds conviction vote and what removal means

Impeachment is an accusation, not an eviction. When the House of Representatives impeaches a president or a federal judge, that official stays in office. Removal can come only later, and only if the Senate votes to convict. That distinction is the one most often blurred in headlines, cable segments and social media posts whenever the word starts trending.

The U.S. Constitution splits the job between the two chambers of Congress by design. The House acts something like a grand jury, deciding whether the evidence justifies formal charges. The Senate acts as the court, hearing the case and delivering a verdict. Each chamber has its own vote threshold, its own procedures and its own political pressures. An official can be impeached by the first and still be acquitted by the second.

The process is rare, but it is not theoretical. The House has impeached presidents four times, and three different men have faced a Senate trial as a result. None was removed. Federal judges are a different story: they are the only officials the Senate has ever convicted. Another president left office before the full House could vote at all.

The Constitution sketches the process in a few short clauses. Much of the detail has been filled in by practice. The House writes its own rules for investigating. The Senate sets its own procedures for trying cases. The Constitution never defines the key phrase describing impeachable conduct, and Congress has interpreted it case by case.

Understanding how impeachment works makes those open questions easier to follow. The 10 slides ahead walk through the process in order. They start with what the word means under the Constitution and who can be impeached. They then cover the grounds for charges, how the House opens an inquiry and how it votes on articles. Next come the Senate trial, the two-thirds bar for conviction and the penalties that follow a conviction. The final slides look back at the presidents who have been impeached. They also compare impeachment with two other routes by which a president can lose power: the 25th Amendment and resignation.

Each slide stands on its own. A reader can go straight to the stage of the process that matters most to them.

Impeachment is the formal act of charging a federal official with misconduct. It is not the act of removing that person from office. Under the U.S. Constitution, the House of Representatives brings the charges, and the Senate decides whether they hold up at trial.

News coverage and everyday conversation often use the word loosely, as if it meant being thrown out of office. That reading skips a step. An official who has been impeached has been accused, much as a criminal defendant who has been indicted stands accused. Neither has been found guilty of anything yet.

The comparison to a criminal case holds only in broad outline. Impeachment is a constitutional proceeding run by Congress, not a prosecution in a courtroom. The two chambers set many of their own procedures for it.

The House's authority comes from Article I, Section 2 of the Constitution. That clause gives the House "the sole Power of Impeachment." No other body can bring the charges.

The Senate's role comes from Article I, Section 3. That section gives the Senate "the sole Power to try all Impeachments." Only the Senate can hold the trial, and only the Senate can deliver the verdict.

Both clauses sit in Article I, the part of the Constitution that establishes Congress. That placement puts impeachment in the hands of the legislature. Courts and the executive branch do not bring the charges or decide the outcome.

The split between the two chambers has a practical consequence. An impeachment by the House, on its own, does not change whether the official holds the job. The person stays in office while the Senate considers the case. If the Senate acquits, the official keeps the position. The impeachment itself still remains part of the official record.

This two-stage design is the core of the process. Every later step — the inquiry, the vote on charges, the trial and any penalty — follows from the division of labor written into those two sections of Article I.

The Constitution allows Congress to impeach the president, the vice president and civil officers of the U.S. government. That coverage, set out in Article II, Section 4, also reaches federal judges. Members of Congress, by contrast, are generally not treated as civil officers who can be impeached.

The presidency draws the most attention, but it is one office among several on the list. Article II, Section 4 places the vice president in the same clause as the president. The two highest executive offices therefore face an identical process. Beyond them, the clause extends to the wider category of civil officers serving in the federal government.

Federal judges hold a distinct place on that list. Their position differs from that of elected officials in one basic way. Article III says federal judges hold office during good behavior. That language gives them no fixed term and no reelection campaign to face. Impeachment gives Congress a constitutional route to end that tenure.

The status of lawmakers was tested early in the country's history. In 1797, the House impeached Senator William Blount. The Senate dismissed the case in 1799 on jurisdictional grounds. A dismissal on those grounds turns on whether the Senate had authority over the case, not on whether the accusations were true.

Rank offers no protection under Article II, Section 4. The clause covers the most senior official in the executive branch, and nothing in its text shields any covered officeholder because of seniority. What the clause does limit is the basis for an impeachment. It ties the process to stated grounds, not to the importance of the person accused.

That structure gives the clause two separate filters. The first asks whether a person holds one of the covered offices. The second asks whether the conduct at issue fits the grounds the Constitution names. Both questions apply to every case brought under the clause.

The Constitution allows impeachment on three grounds: treason, bribery and "other high crimes and misdemeanors." It never defines that last phrase. Congress has given it meaning one case at a time.

The list appears in Article II, Section 4. That clause names the officials who can face impeachment and, in the same sentence, the conduct that can lead to it.

Treason and bribery are named outright. The third category works differently. No clause anywhere in the constitutional text supplies a definition, and no list of qualifying offenses accompanies it. A reader looking for a checklist of impeachable conduct will not find one in the document.

That gap leaves interpretation to Congress. When the House weighs articles of impeachment, its members decide whether the conduct described fits the phrase. When the Senate holds a trial, senators reach their own judgment on the same question. Each vote reflects how individual members read the phrase. The same conduct can draw different answers from different lawmakers.

One question has stayed open: whether an impeachable act must also be an indictable crime. An indictable crime is one that could be charged in a criminal court. Scholars and lawmakers have disagreed on this point. One reading limits the phrase to conduct that breaks a criminal law. Another treats it as broad enough to reach conduct that is not a crime. The Constitution does not resolve the dispute.

The two readings lead to different kinds of charges. Under the narrower reading, an article of impeachment would need to describe conduct that a prosecutor could also take to a criminal court. Under the broader reading, an article could rest on conduct such as a misuse of an office's powers, even where no criminal statute covers it.

The disagreement shapes how impeachment debates unfold. A defense that a charge describes no crime is an argument about this phrase. So is a claim that an official's conduct warrants removal whether or not it breaks a criminal law. Both depend on how members of Congress read a single phrase in Article II, Section 4.

An impeachment inquiry begins in the House of Representatives, where any member can introduce a resolution calling for an official to be impeached. The House Judiciary Committee has usually taken charge of the investigation that follows, though the Constitution sets no fixed procedure for this stage.

Filing a resolution is only a starting point. It does not charge anyone, and it does not commit the House to act. A single lawmaker can put one forward, but the chamber decides whether anything comes of it.

The committee's task at this stage is to establish what happened. It holds hearings and gathers evidence, building the factual record that any later charges would rest on.

The full House can also step in directly. Members can vote to authorize an inquiry, putting the chamber's formal backing behind the investigation.

The Constitution is silent on how any of this should be done. It gives the House the power to impeach but says nothing about who investigates, how evidence is collected or what steps must come before a vote. The House fills that gap itself by setting its own rules.

That arrangement means the inquiry stage is shaped by the chamber's choices rather than by a constitutional script. One inquiry can begin with a member's resolution and committee hearings. Another can begin with a floor vote authorizing the investigation. Both paths fit within the House's authority.

The inquiry is also distinct from what comes later. It is a fact-finding phase, not a trial, and it produces no verdict. No official is impeached during an inquiry. Impeachment itself happens only when the full House approves formal charges.

For readers following an impeachment in the news, the word "inquiry" marks this early, investigative step. It signals that the House is examining an official's conduct. It does not mean the House has decided to bring charges, and it does not mean the official faces removal.

The House impeaches an official by approving at least one article of impeachment, the formal written charge against that person. Each article needs a simple majority of House members voting. If all 435 members cast a vote, 218 votes are enough to pass an article.

Each article sets out one specific allegation of misconduct against the named official. A single impeachment resolution can carry one article or several.

The House does not vote on the package as a whole. Members vote on each article on its own. That allows a lawmaker to support one charge and oppose another. It also means a resolution can leave the House with some articles approved and others rejected.

The majority standard is tied to members voting, not to the full size of the chamber. The 218 figure applies only when all 435 seats are filled and every member votes. A vacant seat, after a death or resignation, cannot cast a vote. When fewer members take part, the number needed for a majority falls with them. If 410 members vote, for example, 206 votes would pass an article. A tie vote fails. A majority means more than half of the votes cast.

Approval of one article is enough. Once an article passes, the official has been impeached, regardless of what the Senate later decides.

After the vote, the House names managers to carry the case forward. The managers are themselves members of the House. They act as prosecutors once the matter moves to the Senate. They present the charges contained in the approved articles and argue for conviction.

Only the articles that win a majority travel to the Senate. The House delivers the approved articles to the Senate, which then organizes the trial. A charge the House rejects is not part of the impeachment. The Senate does not weigh it at trial.

A Senate impeachment trial turns senators into jurors who weigh the House's charges and decide whether to convict. House managers argue the case, the official's defense team answers it, and the Senate votes on each article separately.

That jury role begins with an oath or affirmation. Every senator takes one before hearing the case. Outside a trial, senators debate and pass legislation. During one, they sit in judgment of a specific official on specific charges. The affirmation exists as an alternative for senators who prefer not to swear an oath.

Who presides depends on who is on trial. When the president is the defendant, Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution requires the chief justice of the Supreme Court to preside. That requirement applies only to presidential trials. It places the head of the federal judiciary in the chair.

The prosecution comes from the House. Its case is presented by House members known as impeachment managers. In the Senate chamber, those managers lay out the evidence and arguments behind each charge. The accused official is represented by a defense team, which responds to the managers and argues for acquittal. Senators hear both sides before any vote is taken.

The verdict is not a single up-or-down vote on the whole case. Senators vote on each article on its own. The result can differ from one charge to the next. A conviction on any single article is enough to convict the official, even if the other articles fail. Each conviction vote requires two-thirds of the senators present.

Federal courts have left these procedures to the Senate. In Nixon v. United States, decided in 1993, the Supreme Court held that challenges to the Senate's trial procedures were nonjusticiable. In practical terms, that means courts will not hear such disputes. The Senate decides for itself how to run an impeachment trial. The case involved Judge Walter Nixon, not President Richard Nixon.

Convicting an impeached official takes the votes of two-thirds of the senators present, a requirement written into Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution. When all 100 senators vote, at least 67 must vote to convict.

The threshold is measured against attendance, not against the full size of the chamber. An absent senator does not count toward the base used to calculate two-thirds. If 99 senators are present, conviction takes 66 votes. If 98 are present, 65 votes would fall just short of two-thirds, so conviction still takes 66.

The same math shows how few votes it takes to stop a conviction. With every senator voting, 34 votes against an article are enough to defeat it. The blocking number stays at 34 when 99 senators are present, because 66 votes would still be needed to convict. That means a bloc of just over one-third of the chamber can end the case on that charge.

The Senate standard sits well above the simple majority the House uses to impeach. The same two-thirds standard applies whether the accused official is a president, a federal judge or another civil officer.

The higher Senate number has a political consequence. Conviction generally requires votes from senators of both parties. For one party to convict on its own, it would need at least 67 seats, with all 100 senators present and every member of that party voting together.

Seat counts show how much cross-party support a conviction needs. A party holding 50 seats, with all 100 senators present, would need at least 17 votes from outside its ranks. A party holding 60 seats would still need seven. In practice, the side pressing for conviction has to persuade members of the opposing party.

That threshold has never been reached in a presidential case. No president has been convicted by the Senate.

If no article reaches two-thirds, the official is acquitted on every charge and keeps the job.

A Senate conviction removes the official from office. The Senate can also bar that person from holding federal office in the future. The Constitution allows no other penalty in an impeachment case.

Article I, Section 3 limits judgment in cases of impeachment to removal from office and disqualification from holding federal office. The Senate cannot impose a fine, order prison time or seize property as part of an impeachment judgment. An impeachment trial decides whether someone may hold federal office. It does not decide whether that person is punished as a criminal.

Removal comes with the conviction itself. Once the Senate convicts on an article, the official loses the office.

Disqualification works differently. It is optional, and the Senate has decided it through a separate vote. That vote has required only a simple majority. The case of Judge Thomas Porteous shows how the two steps fit together. The Senate removed Porteous from the federal bench in 2010. Then, in its own vote, it barred him from holding future federal office.

The two penalties do different things. Removal ends the official's time in their current post. Disqualification looks forward and closes off future federal office.

Leaving office through impeachment does not end the possibility of criminal charges. Article I, Section 3 states that the convicted party remains "liable and subject to Indictment, Trial, Judgment and Punishment, according to Law." Prosecutors may bring an ordinary criminal case over the same conduct. Such a case would run through the regular courts under criminal law, not under Senate trial rules.

The president's pardon power has a specific limit here. Article II, Section 2 lets the president grant reprieves and pardons for offenses against the U.S., "except in Cases of Impeachment." A president cannot use a pardon to undo an impeachment or reverse a Senate conviction. No pardon can restore a removed official to office or lift a bar on future federal service.

Three U.S. presidents have been impeached by the House of Representatives: Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton and Donald Trump. The Senate acquitted all three men every time, and none was removed from office.

Andrew Johnson was the first. The House impeached him in 1868, which sent the case to the Senate for trial. Senators acquitted him by a single vote. One more vote to convict would have removed him from office.

Johnson's case stood alone for 130 years. The House did not impeach another president until 1998.

That president was Bill Clinton. The House impeached him on December 19, 1998. His Senate trial ran into the next year. Senators acquitted Clinton on February 12, 1999, less than two months after the House vote. He stayed in office. He remains the only president impeached in the 20th century.

Donald Trump became the third impeached president about 21 years after Clinton. The House first impeached him in December 2019. The Senate acquitted him on February 5, 2020.

The House impeached Trump again on January 13, 2021, roughly 13 months after the first time. The Senate acquitted him one month later, on February 13, 2021. Trump is the only president to face two impeachments. They came in consecutive years, the shortest gap between any two presidential impeachments.

The second trial centered on a single article of impeachment. Senators voted 57 to 43. A majority of the chamber sided with conviction. The tally still fell short of the two-thirds threshold the Constitution sets for a guilty verdict.

Richard Nixon is absent from this list because the full House never voted to impeach him.

Federal judges have a different record. They are the only federal officials the Senate has convicted. The House has impeached 15 federal judges, and eight of them were convicted. The other seven ended without a conviction. No presidential impeachment has ended that way.

Impeachment charges an official with misconduct. The 25th Amendment addresses a president who cannot do the job, and resignation is a voluntary exit. The three are often mentioned together, but they work in different ways and serve different purposes.

The 25th Amendment was ratified in 1967. It governs presidential disability and succession. Its focus is whether the president is able to serve, not how the president has behaved in office.

Section 4 of the amendment allows the vice president and a majority of the cabinet to declare that the president is unable to serve. That decision starts inside the executive branch. Impeachment, by contrast, begins with charges brought by the House of Representatives.

The 25th Amendment is not a punishment process. It does not accuse the president of wrongdoing. It involves no articles, no prosecutors and no trial. An impeachment, on the other hand, is a formal accusation that an official has committed an offense serious enough to justify removal. The 25th Amendment applies only to the president, while impeachment reaches the vice president, federal judges and other civil officers as well.

Resignation works differently from both. When an official steps down, the impeachment process usually ends without a Senate verdict. No senator votes to convict or acquit. The question of guilt is never formally resolved.

Richard Nixon followed this path. He resigned on August 9, 1974. By then, the House Judiciary Committee had approved articles of impeachment against him. The full House never held a floor vote on those articles. Nixon was never impeached by the full House.

Resignation does not always stop Congress, though. In 1876, the House impeached William Belknap, the former secretary of war, despite his resignation. The case went to a Senate trial, and the Senate acquitted him.

Of the three routes, impeachment is the only one that runs through both chambers of Congress. It is also the only one that ends in a vote on specific charges.

#5445. Claude can now join video calls as an active, visible teammate in Anthropic’s latest push to reinvent white collar jobs beyond coding

Anthropic ‘s Claude Code reinvented the field of software engineering, turning AI into a must-have tool for programmers. Now the company is seeking to do the same across the corporate workplace with a new suite of office productivity tools launched on Tuesday.

The new products are an important part of Anthropic’s effort to broaden its base of paying customers and boost its revenue as it moves closer to a widely-anticipated initial public stock offering. The IPO, which could value Anthropic at roughly $1.4 trillion, is scheduled for as soon as next week, the company revealed separately on Tuesday.

To help create momentum around the product launch, Anthropic held a buzzy launch event in San Francisco Tuesday with hundreds of guests. Anthropic’s Chief Product Officer Ami Vora spoke on stage about how Claude has changed computer coding over the past year. Engineers can now delegate entire tasks to AI, but at the same time the work for most other teams has largely stayed the same, save for perhaps an email getting written faster, or a meeting being summarized.

The new products aim to bring the same AI benefits programmers have enjoyed “for over a year,” Vora said, to knowledge workers across corporations. Anthropic’s renewed push to attract corporate knowledge workers could put the company in closer competition with other software vendors such as Microsoft, whose shares were down more than 2% after the news was announced.

Anthropic’s vision is to turn Claude into an active member a team, rather than an optimization tool for individuals. For example, with Claude Meetings, professionals can add Claude to video calls as a “visible participant,” Anthropic said. The AI listens to the conversation and can “start on the work while people are still talking.” It lays out the proposed plan and timeline, answers questions in the call chat, and handles tasks such as pulling up last year’s numbers, using “the work apps people have connected,” Anthropic said. The results surface in claude.ai after the call.

Claude Meetings is in beta for Team and Enterprise plans, and starting with Google Meet, with plans to expand to other video platforms.

With Claude Whiteboards, humans can brainstorm ideas and collaborate with Claude. “A team talks through a messy plan out loud, and Claude turns it into a board with a timeline, owners and dates,” Anthropic said. Same goes for Claude Sheets, which are spreadsheets teams can build and edit alongside Claude, and can export to Excel or CSV files. Both these products are also in beta.

If these products can automate a meaningful portion of non-coding roles, they could encourage more businesses to sign up for Claude subscription plans. However, they could also create mayhem or burn tokens on AI-generated materials that never get used.

Anthropic is also seeking ways to deeply embed Claude in critical business functions. Another product called Claude Data, formerly Claude Dashboards, connects the AI to systems where companies keep their most important numbers, such as a data warehouse or CRM. Claude Data became available for paid plans today.

Similarly, new Claude Connectors “link Claude to the apps a company already uses, so Claude can pull information from them and take actions in them,” Anthropic said. Over 9,000 apps are available as Claude Connectors, such as Salesforce and Workday. “Teams already do much of their work in apps like these,” Anthropic said. “Now they can open the full app beside the conversation and ask Claude to work in it with them.” That means “no more switching tabs,” said Nicholas Lin, who leads product for knowledge work at Anthropic, on stage at today’s event.

Tuesday’s launch event came on the same day as Anthropic kicked off its pre-IPO roadshow with investors.

The idea of Claude revolutionizing non-coding roles in the same way it’s done for coding could energize the IPO and drive up the share price. Several sources we spoke to think Anthropic’s $70-$78 target share price is intentionally low, a tactic to set expectations and leave room to shatter them.

“Anthropic is moving forward with its IPO at a steeper discount than market initially anticipated,” said Lior Prosor, managing partner of Deep33, a deep-tech venture fund. “We think that is a smart pricing strategy. It gives nervous ‘AI-trade’ investors meaningful potential upside while securing the capital Anthropic needs to take full control of its destiny and fund its compute commitments.”

Also this week, Anthropic debuted new frontier models, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, at a lower price with allegedly stronger performance than OpenAI’s latest frontier model, GPT-6 Astra. This also got investors’ attention.

“Anthropic has shown incredible advances recently and their announcement about Fable 5.2 yesterday suggests they could have a bigger impact in hardware domains like robotics than people might have given them credit for previously,” said Bastiaan Janmaat, General Partner at Lithos Capital.

#5444. Let there be LEDs: Tech upgrade helps James Turrell’s Skyspace shine again at UW art museum

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:01 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:42 am

For most of the past dozen years, a James Turrell artwork on the University of Washington campus in Seattle — built to glow at sunrise and sunset — has been running on daylight alone.

That changes Nov. 14, when UW’s Henry Art Gallery relights “Light Reign,” its Turrell Skyspace, after a restoration that replaced aging lights with hundreds of new fixtures and a control system synced to the sun.

Originally installed in 2003 near the Henry’s entrance along 15th Avenue N.E., “Light Reign” is one of dozens of skyspaces by Turrell, the 83-year-old artist known for turning light itself into his medium.

Inside the artwork’s oval chamber, LEDs bathe the walls in slowly shifting color, and when the weather cooperates, a retractable lid opens to an oculus that frames the sky. From outside, the glass-paneled shell lights up with its own program — a 21st-century mood ring just steps from a bronze George Washington who has been gazing west toward the Olympics since 1909.

The relighting comes as the Henry, Washington’s first public art museum, heads into its 100th year. The museum opened on campus in February 1927, and officials are hinting that bigger changes are on the way for the centennial.

Trouble with “Light Reign” started around 2015, said Sage Sommer, the Henry’s director of exhibitions and collections. The original lights, by then more than a decade old, were reaching the end of their lifespan, and over time the museum lost the ability to run them.

Through those years, the Skyspace stayed open. Visitors could still sit inside, meditate and watch clouds and birds pass over the oculus, just without the color.

After years of planning, the Henry settled on a full lighting overhaul that also folds in ideas Turrell has used in his newer skyspaces. The exterior already ran on LEDs, but a very early generation of them, while the interior and oculus were lit by neon tubes made by Western Neon.

The museum didn’t work with Turrell directly. Instead it worked with lighting designer Ryan Pike, whose company, RHMP, works only on Turrell installations, from upgrades of existing pieces to new projects. Pike has worked on Turrell artworks since 2013.

For Pike, the toughest part was the exterior. “It’s just over 700 lights, in nine DMX universes, so each fixture can output independently of the rest,” he said in an email. DMX is the standard protocol for controlling stage and architectural lighting. Splitting the facade across multiple universes lets every fixture be programmed on its own.

Sommer said the Skyspace isn’t strictly time-based media, a museum term for art that relies on equipment and unfolds over time. But it raises the same questions. Sometimes the fix is simple, like converting a VHS tape to a digital file. Other times the hardware is integral to the work. Some artists insist a piece be shown only on a CRT TV, and some come back with a remastered version and want only that one shown.

“We work really closely with the artists to make sure that it is as they envision,” she said.

The Henry isn’t the only museum to face the problem. In 2023, Minneapolis’ Walker Art Center restored its own Turrell skyspace, “Sky Pesher,” after it became impossible to find the cold cathode tubes — a 1920s-era technology — that powered its sunrise and sunset lighting program.

Working with Turrell and his studio, the Walker switched to LEDs, which allowed more control and a much wider range of color. What had been “shades of tinted white” is now multicolored, Joe King, the Walker’s director of collections and exhibition management, said in an interview published by the museum.

The Henry’s new system uses roughly 840 LED fixtures, about 710 outside and 130 inside, Sommer said. The exterior program kicks in a half-hour before dawn and dusk. The morning show is brief, about 36 minutes, while the evening one currently runs about four hours after sunset.

“The very cool thing about this space, because we are so far north, is just how connected to sunrise and sunset it is, and how drastically different it is throughout the year,” Sommer said.

The roof has its own engineering pedigree. The Skyspace’s hydraulic lid, which lifts and slides out of the way, was designed by submarine manufacturers in Everett. It stays shut in the rain.

The museum closed the Skyspace in late July and used the downtime for physical restoration, too: repainting the interior, refinishing the teak benches, waxing floors, replacing worn locks, refitting doors that had swollen and cleaning out the gutters. Everything had to be rewired, and the project took longer than expected.

“Light Reign” is the most visible piece in the Henry’s collection of about 30,000 objects, including more than 18,000 textiles and 7,000 works on paper. Only a sliver is ever on view, so the Henry is putting its collection database online. The project was funded by UW’s Student Technology Fee. Anyone can book an appointment at its study center to see a piece up close.

Technology is also the focus of the Henry’s centennial exhibition, opening in late February. Swagato Chakravorty, associate curator, said he was surprised that no major museum had mounted a large, ambitious show on contemporary art and technology in decades, even as Seattle was transformed around it. His show looks at technology “from below,” focusing on the people and communities most directly affected rather than a “great man” story.

The exhibition is loosely organized around three threads. One is bioethics, including a work the Henry commissioned in 2002 with UW geneticist Mary-Claire King, which is being revived 25 years later. Another pairs Indigenous knowledge with tools like 3D printing and algorithms. The third is technology’s material toll, from data centers to water use.

Chakravorty said he deliberately avoids taking a side on whether technology is good or bad for art.

“Writing is a technology. Cave painting was a technology,” he said. As for AI: “It’s not going to kill art.”

The public unveiling of the refurbished “Light Reign” runs 3:30 to 6 p.m. Nov. 14, with remarks from Henry Executive Director Kris Lewis and the exterior illumination starting at 4 p.m. Admission is free, though the Henry encourages RSVPs, and interior viewing is limited to 25 people at a time for about 10 minutes each.

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
