#5427. 2 scandals, 1 destination—Why Nvidia can’t shake China smuggling allegations

For more than a year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeated the party line about covert smuggling of his highly coveted premium chips: There’s no evidence Nvidia AI chips are being diverted to China, Huang has asserted.

But now two bombshell scandals, both allegedly running through Southeast Asia, have blasted a data-center sized hole through Huang’s credibility. The first case, in which $2.5 billion in computer servers equipped with Nvidia chips are under scrutiny, involves Super Micro, a company led by a longtime friend of Jensen Huang’s and one of Nvidia’s closest partners. More recently, a separate string of reports has revealed that Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian customer, Megaspeed, is under U.S. investigation for chip diversion.

There is no evidence so far that the two cases are directly connected, though some industry observers have pointed to potential areas of overlap. Whether the two cases are ultimately determined to be part of a larger scheme, or completely separate incidents, the dual scandals have left Nvidia, shareholders, and its famous CEO, reeling.

On Sunday, Huang told employees in an email he had betrayed his wife and family in an extramarital affair. His confession followed reports claiming that intelligence officials believe Huang’s affair partner, Alice Huang (no relation), was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to purportedly report on his doings to Beijing. Alice Huang is a former executive of Megaspeed International, a Singapore company that reportedly became Nvidia’s largest chip buyer in Southeast Asia.

Alongside Huang’s admission, Nvidia’s board announced it has opened an independent investigation into whether Nvidia co-founder Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence operation but noted that board members maintain “confidence” in Huang. The board said it has no reason to believe that “either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Nvidia board members have retained acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run point on the investigation, Nvidia announced Tuesday.

Nvidia’s GPU chips are critical components for training and running advanced AI models such as those made by OpenAI and Anthropic. The U.S. government considers the chips to be dual-use technology with potential military applications, and requires specific export licenses to sell them to countries such as China—which haven’t been granted to Nvidia’s most high-powered chips.

How things will shake out for Nvidia is evolving in real time, but it’s likely that a terse letter Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) sent to Nvidia in June will turn into a subpoena. That’s thanks to midterm election results that saw Democrats regain the Senate with Warren poised to chair the powerful Senate Banking Committee in January. Warren and Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) called Monday for Nvidia to answer questions, and three House committee chairs have asked Huang to accede to a closed-door grilling before lawmakers November 18, the day after Nvidia is scheduled to report its third quarter financial results.

The June letter, which went to Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter and audit committee chair Brooke Seawell, sought answers from Nvidia regarding the state of its compliance program and noted that Nvidia continued to include Super Micro Computer (Supermicro) as a key partner in its network. The letter also cited Culper Research, a short seller who bet against Nvidia and published a report that alleges possible smuggling links between Supermicro, Nvidia, and Megaspeed, the company where Alice Huang was a top executive. U.S. authorities have investigated whether the billions in Nvidia hardware Megaspeed bought through Nvidia’s server partners went to Chinese firms barred from getting the chips. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing.

Alice Huang is now the link between the CEO infidelity and coverup scandal facing Jensen Huang, the poster CEO for the AI buildout, and a question that has persistently dogged Nvidia, which is where its chips actually wind up after they’re purchased. And as far as export control compliance goes, an alleged honey trap espionage case carries a lot more public-interest tailwind than the at times byzantine regulations involved in obtaining and complying with export restrictions and licensing. Meaning, this latest revelation is unlikely to blow over as a single rogue actor or administrative export record issue.

One export-control veteran, who asked to speak anonymously because of his clients, said if he were an independent director or general counsel, he’d be looking at whether the company they oversee has a Huang honeytrap problem—and not just at the CEO level. Executives who are supposed to inspect data centers or conduct due diligence have been the targets of these types of seduction schemes going back decades.

He also nodded to the March Supermicro indictment that pointed out that a compliance auditor was “off-site enjoying entertainment paid for by” another company. It’s a fairly common tactic, he said.

Until recently, the most high-profile case of contraband Nvidia chips involved one of Nvidia’s closest partners, a company run by Huang’s longtime friend, Supermicro CEO Charles Liang. Neither Liang nor Supermicro was charged and Supermicro has said it is cooperating with authorities. Liang and Huang, who both founded their respective companies in 1993, often took the stage together at an event called Computex in Taiwan and joked back and forth during their joint keynotes.

“When we’re together, sometimes we speak Taiwanese, sometimes we speak Mandarin, and then when we disagree, we speak English,” Huang joked before an adoring crowd at Computex in 2024. (Huang was photographed with Alice Huang, his affair partner, at a Taipei cocktail bar during Computex that year.)

In March, federal prosecutors charged Supermicro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and two others with routing about $2.5 billion in servers laden with Nvidia H200 and B200 GPUs to China via a Southeast Asian front company. Supermicro was not charged and has said it was a victim of the scheme. Liaw has pleaded not guilty, although one of the three who were charged pleaded guilty last month. Liaw cofounded Supermicro with Liang and Liang’s wife, Sara Liu the same year Huang co-founded Nvidia. Neither Liang nor Liu were named in the indictment.

According to Liaw’s indictment, the elaborate scheme involved staging thousands of nonworking dummy servers in three warehouses to trick auditors. Contractors used hair dryers to soften the adhesive on serial-number labels and peel them off. That alleged scheme followed a similar playbook as one that had ensnared Supermicro in 2006, when the company pleaded guilty to illegally exporting computer equipment to Iran through a distributor in Dubai. Both routes involved selling to a neighboring country to keep the real buyer hidden.

The Liaw indictment does not accuse Nvidia of wrongdoing, but it lays out how the front company’s orders for Supermicro hardware fed into Nvidia’s chip allocation. In December 2024, Liaw allegedly asked the front company for monthly forecasts, writing that the forecasts were “the only way” to get Nvidia to promise B200 chip allocations, according to the indictment. Bloomberg later reported and Culper agreed that the front company in the alleged scheme is OBON, a Bangkok AI infrastructure firm. OBON has not been charged.

Supermicro has since disclosed that it received a grand jury subpoena from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, subpoenas and inquiries from foreign authorities, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the Bureau of Industry and Security. In Liaw’s case, his lawyer told the judge the documents Supermicro would give the government could be material to his defense, and his trial was pushed back from November 2026 to March 2027.

As details of the Megaspeed scandal emerge, Nvidia’s chips are now at the center of a second major smuggling case—this time involving one of its own customers. Megaspeed reportedly bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips during the past two years, with nearly $2 billion of the chips installed in data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia that are alleged to serve Chinese customers remotely, according to New York Times reporting.

Nvidia, in what could become a grave misstep, repeatedly assured the public that Megaspeed was credible. In October 2025, a spokesperson said Nvidia had visited Megaspeed operations and found no evidence of chip diversion. Last month, as reports about suspected Chinese spying emerged, Nvidia said the diversion allegations against Megaspeed had been “thoroughly investigated and debunked.” Jensen Huang, in a statement that has depreciated faster than an older-generation GPU, told Bloomberg his interactions with Alice Huang were “completely normal and not unusual.”

In May, Culper Research, which has shorted Nvidia, argued there were connections between the Supermicro indictment, alleged Nvidia chip smuggling, and Megaspeed. Culper wrote that Megaspeed’s website once listed Supermicro as a partner alongside Nvidia, Intel, and Gigabyte. The web entry was removed, but it still sits in the site code, Culper found. In addition, the report called the reported Supermicro-OBON smuggling route one of many that Nvidia chips travel before they get to China.

Huang next faces analysts on Nov. 17, when Nvidia reports third quarter earnings. The following day, House lawmakers have asked for a closed-door briefing. And in January, Warren is expected to wield the subpoena power of the Banking Committee and get the answers she originally sought back in June.

Amanda Gerut is the west coast editor at Fortune, overseeing publicly traded businesses, executive compensation, Securities and Exchange Commission regulations, and investigations.

#5426. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5425. Restaurant Chains Are Hungry for a Comeback. Can This Change Bring Diners Back?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Popular restaurants want customers back, and they’re rethinking their core offerings to win their business.

Restaurant chains are putting their menus front and center as they work to bring back customers.

The push comes as Americans eat out less often and become more selective about what they spend their money on, according to Black Box Intelligence data cited in a new CNBC report. On quarterly earnings calls in recent weeks, executives at Wendy’s, Chipotle Mexican Grill and other chains highlighted changes already reaching customers or headed to menus.

Discounts and limited-time deals can draw a crowd, but chains are counting on taste and quality to turn those visits into repeat business. Additionally, corporate chefs are taking a bigger role in the fight for diners as companies look for an edge beyond promotions.

At Chipotle, that includes another run for its limited-time brisket, which returned to menus last week.

“We think the product’s improved and even better,” CEO Scott Boatwright told analysts on the company’s late-October earnings call.

At Wendy’s, a menu overhaul is part of a broader effort to boost sales. The chain unveiled a five-part turnaround plan last week, which includes a pledge to deliver “quality food at real value.”

CEO Bob Wright told analysts that Wendy’s is testing changes to some of its staples, including thicker, crispier bacon, a richer and creamier Frosty, whole-leaf lettuce for sandwiches and revamped salads.

“We’re also rebuilding our food offerings and have begun testing improvements to quality and craveability of our core items,” he said.

The chain is intent on winning back customers as it contends with lackluster sales. Last week, Wendy’s reported a seventh consecutive quarter of declining same-store sales.

A recipe overhaul can help revive a restaurant business. For example, Domino’s rebuilt its pizza offering in 2009 with a new sauce, garlic-seasoned crust and improved cheese combination. The company then aired candid ads acknowledging complaints that its old crust tasted like cardboard and its sauce resembled ketchup. The recipe changes and marketing push helped drive a 9.9% increase in Domino’s U.S. same-store sales in 2010, per CNBC.

Now, some of the people behind the Domino’s comeback are using the same playbook at Burger King’s U.S. locations.

At Burger King, improvements to menu staples are a central piece of its multiyear turnaround effort. The chain began with the Whopper earlier this year, introducing an upgraded bun and new mayonnaise. In September, it turned to chicken nuggets, rolling out a version made with 100% white meat, crunchier breading and a more flavorful marinade, alongside reformulated sauces.

“We’ve tried to look at our biggest categories first,” Josh Kobza, CEO of Burger King parent Restaurant Brands International, told CNBC.

The effort is paying off. Burger King reported an 8.4% increase in U.S. same-store sales for the third quarter. Sales of the Whopper rose by a double-digit percentage, while chicken nugget sales surged more than 35%, Kobza told analysts on the company’s late-October earnings call.

#5423. This Founder Went From ‘Kitchen Chemist’ to 9-Figure Business Owner Whose Products Are Sold at Target, Ulta and CVS

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Janell Stephens started her career as a speech language pathologist before tapping into her passion for haircare.

Janell Stephens started haircare brand Camille Rose in her kitchen in 2011 to create hair products that worked for her family. Her experimentation became the foundation for a brand now found in major retailers including Target, Ulta and CVS.

“I call myself a kitchen chemist,” Stephens, founder and CEO of Camille Rose, said in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “I was just in the kitchen making a plethora of products at the time.”

Stephens built the company gradually, moving from homemade products to working with chemists, manufacturers, marketers, warehouse staff and a broader team of 35 employees. This year, the company is on track for 9-figure revenue, and projects continued double-digit growth in 2027.

The brand had a breakout moment earlier this year when reality TV star Kim Kardashian used Camille Rose products to style her 8-year-old daughter Chicago’s hair.

Stephens is a speech language pathologist by training. Before starting Camille Rose, she worked with stroke survivors and people with swallowing disorders, traumatic brain injuries and speech disorders. After graduate school, she opened a home-health agency and ran it for about eight years.

While her husband completed a medical fellowship in hematology and oncology, Stephens sold her clinic and decided to pursue another long-standing interest: formulating hair and skin products. She began studying under an herbalist for about a year, learning about the properties of oils, herbs and butters, and how different ingredients could perform on hair and skin.

“He taught me about herbs,” she says. “He taught me about the benefits of oils, how to make an emollient, the benefits of different butters and how they would affect or how they would apply to the hair and skin.”

Camille Rose grew from a personal problem. Stephens wanted products that delivered visible results for her own hair and for her children’s hair. At the time, she says, she was paying close attention to what was listed on product labels and was dissatisfied with what she found in the market.

“My kids had needs; I had needs,” Stephens says. “I needed products that were showing a difference in my hair and in their hair, and I was also [reading the labels of] everything that I was using back then.”

Rather than settle for existing options, she began buying ingredients and studying formulations. “From that point on, I became obsessed with it,” Stephens says. “I just found it so fascinating, finding, ordering different ingredients, trying it out. If it works, yes, I’ll keep it. If it doesn’t, throw it out, start over.”

The first product she jarred, labeled and sold was Camille Rose’s Algae Renew Deep Conditioner, made with blue-green algae and vitamins. It remains one of the company’s bestsellers. Another early hit, Curl Love Moisture Milk, remains a central product for the brand.

Stephens refers to the brand’s “core four” as Cocoa Nibs & Honey Growth Serum, Curl Love Moisture Milk, Algae Renew Deep Conditioner and Almond Jai Twisting Butter. But she said she often recommends the deep conditioner as a place for customers to start.

The products also established a signature Camille Rose philosophy: Using food-inspired ingredients and drawing connections between nutrition and personal care.

“If it nourishes your body inside, my philosophy and what I live by is that it should have those same benefits to the outside of the body,” she says.

Sea moss is one example. Stephens noted that consumers use it as a nutritional ingredient because of its mineral content, and she sees a similar potential for products applied externally.

However, she is quick to distinguish her approach from an overly simplistic “all-natural” marketing claim. “We’re not all-natural,” Stephens says. “We never claim all-natural, and I don’t think anybody should.”

Camille Rose uses natural and naturally derived ingredients, but it also uses preservatives. That distinction matters, particularly in beauty, where a product must maintain stability, safety and performance over time. “You also cannot make one product solely on food-grade ingredients,” Stephens says. “The rest are all ingredients that are science-backed.”

Stephens started making products as a hobby and gave them away to friends and family for free in exchange for feedback. When they kept coming back for more, she decided to put up a website and start taking orders. She used feedback and repeat requests to establish demand.

Stephens launched Camille Rose online in 2011. Orders followed, with growth driven by word-of-mouth, Facebook and customer results. As the business began gaining traction online, Stephens recognized that she needed outside support.

She contacted another beauty brand whose products she had used and asked if she could work with its chemist. The chemist agreed to work with her on a contract basis and helped transform homemade recipes into scalable formulations.

“It went from a pinch of this and a dash of that to real percentages,” Stephens says.

That kind of precision became increasingly important as Camille Rose moved beyond its kitchen origins. Stephens said it took roughly a year and a half to find the manufacturer and chemist relationship that fit the company’s needs and values.

The company’s first major retail breakthrough came at a hair show in 2012, where Stephens set up a booth to introduce Camille Rose to prospective customers and industry contacts. A buyer stopped by, and Stephens was initially unaware which retailer he represented. They spoke for about an hour about the brand’s origins, her reasons for starting it and the purpose behind individual products.

“At the end of that hour, he pulled out his card and he said, ‘I am a buyer from Target. I would love to fly you up,’” Stephens recalls.

The brand launched in100 Target stores. Even at that scale, the orders were demanding. “My first orders were thousands per product, so I was nonstop,” Stephens says.

She called on family and friends to help produce the orders. In the early days, she handled nearly every other task, too: customer service, shipping, packing, social media and operations. “I was my everything,” she says.

As Camille Rose expanded, Stephens moved its operations from her home to a small warehouse, hired an additional person to help formulate products and gradually built a more conventional organization. Today, the business includes employees in marketing, social media, digital, creative, operations, customer service and warehousing.

However, Stephens has remained closely involved in product development. “I’m still a product developer for Camille Rose,” she says. “Of course, I have a lab and a team of chemists and researchers that’s working with me.”

The work is more structured now than it was during the company’s kitchen phase. Developing a new product can take months to a year, Stephens says. She begins with a concept and works with her team to develop, evaluate and refine it.

Stephens tries the products herself and also works with stylists and hair models. The company tests products across different curl types and textures and compares them against established products in the market.

That can mean going back to the lab to improve a formula’s shine, frizz control or overall performance. The goal is to ensure each product meets the brand’s standard.

Maintaining that standard was especially important when Camille Rose began scaling production. “I needed to make sure that my manufacturer and the chemist that I’m working with honored our formulas,” she says.

Camille Rose’s growth has depended on making the brand visible. Stephens says the company leans on social media, influencers and celebrity relationships.

TikTok is a priority for the company. Stephens’s core advice for founders thinking about social media marketing is to simply start.

“Turn the camera on and start talking about your product,” she says. “You may have five people listening; you may have 500 people listening, but keep at it. Turn the camera on.”

For a founder launching a haircare or other product, Stephens said the first 90 days should focus on brand identity, awareness and consistent outreach. That includes developing a strong brand guide, becoming the brand’s own first influencer and using both organic and paid partnerships to build an audience.

She also advocates grassroots marketing: handing out samples at parks and festivals, participating in local markets and speaking directly with shoppers at neighborhood stores.

Stephens urges founders to act consistently, even when the next step appears small.

“If you have an idea, don’t just let it sit out there and don’t just talk about it,” she says. “Write out a plan to do something and move forward.”

#5422. Solana Targets Durable Nonces After $270M Drift Hack as Pump.fun Backlash Grows

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Solana developers are preparing to remove durable nonces, the transaction feature exploited in April’s $270 million Drift Protocol hack. The proposed change marks a major shift in how the network handles offline approvals, with implications for exchanges and institutional custodians.

The proposal, known as SIMD-0723, would retire a mechanism that allows signed transactions to remain valid indefinitely. Attackers reportedly exploited this functionality to execute pre-approved transactions more than a week after obtaining signatures from Drift’s security council.

Solana wants to kill the feature behind April's $270M+ Drift hack.SIMD-0723, filed Nov 5 by Anza, would retire "durable nonces": signed transactions that never expire. Normal Solana transactions go stale in ~30 seconds. Earliest switch-off: May 5, 2027. pic.twitter.com/VYYttCsvJk

The move comes as Solana faces another challenge closer to its retail ecosystem. Pump.fun is facing growing community criticism over platform fees, influencer promotions, and allegations of hidden-wallet trading. Together, the developments put renewed attention on security, transparency and trust across Solana’s ecosystem.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Normal Solana transactions use recent blockhashes that expire after 30 seconds. Durable nonces replace those temporary references with stored values, allowing transactions to remain executable until the nonce advances.

The feature was designed for legitimate operational needs. Exchanges, custodians, and multisig organizations often require offline signing procedures that take longer than Solana’s normal transaction window.

However, attackers turned that convenience into an attack vector against Drift on April 1, 2026. They reportedly secured administrative approvals through air-gapped signing systems before allowing the transactions to sit for more than a week.

Once submitted, the approvals helped attackers take control of the protocol and drain at least $270 million. Drift subsequently attributed the attack to a North Korean-linked group.

Anza contributor Gabe Rodriguez filed SIMD-0723 on November 5. The proposal would require transactions to use recent blockhashes after activation. May 5, 2027, represents the earliest proposed mainnet activation date. The change still requires technical approval and migration planning.

Solana is also exploring replacement programs that could support offline signing without relying on durable nonces. These alternatives would introduce different authorization and transaction-failure considerations for custodians.

The proposal forces institutional users to reconsider how they authorize transactions across Solana. Meanwhile, questions about trust are becoming harder to ignore elsewhere in the ecosystem.

Pump.fun has attracted fresh criticism following several developments involving its business model and influencer ecosystem.

On November 6, blockchain tracker Lookonchain reported that Pump.fun transferred 76,111 SOL, worth approximately $6.85 million, to Kraken. The movement reignited criticism over platform fees and whether its incentives adequately serve ordinary traders.

Pump fun(@Pumpfun) is dumping $SOL again!They just deposited 76,111 $SOL ($6.85M) into #Kraken.In total, https://t.co/TcwYRTArT2 has sold 5,553,833 $SOL($882.4M) at an average price of $158.88.https://t.co/kyztoJLCjt pic.twitter.com/QvzqaR8fGI

Bubblemaps also accused prominent influencers of using undisclosed wallets to purchase tokens before publicly recommending them. Its investigations estimated $125,000 in combined trading profits and promotional rewards involving influencer Ethan.

Separate allegations involving paid streamer collaborations surfaced on November 7. The revelations have intensified questions about transparency within Pump.fun’s promotional ecosystem.

These controversies involve different problems from Drift’s exploit, but they expose a similar challenge: maintaining confidence among participants.

That challenge also creates an interesting opportunity for Bitcoin-focused projects exploring alternative execution environments.

Bitcoin Hyper is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 using Solana Virtual Machine technology. Its architecture aims to combine SVM’s high-speed execution with Bitcoin-based settlement, bringing smart contracts, decentralized exchanges, and staking functionality to BTC.

Bitcoin Hyper is not simply another Solana application. Its design uses SVM execution while anchoring Layer 2 state to Bitcoin through periodic commitments and zero-knowledge proofs.

This combination gives it a different proposition from Solana-native applications. Developers can work with an execution environment associated with Solana’s performance, while the project targets Bitcoin’s established settlement infrastructure.

Bitcoin Hyper has also reached several development milestones. Its testnet is live, with a public explorer allowing users to inspect transactions and network activity.

The project’s presale has raised approximately $33.2 million, with HYPER priced at a low $0.0136 per coin. Its November 26 presale deadline leaves 17 days from today for prospective participants to enter before the planned launch window.

The upcoming transition toward mainnet, wallet infrastructure, and exchange listings puts the project in an important stage of development. Its combination of Bitcoin settlement and SVM execution gives it a distinct position in the expanding Bitcoin Layer 2 sector.

#5421. Trevor Noah on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 8, 2026 at 9:52 amNovember 8, 2026 at 9:52 am

On Oct. 19, Trevor Noah launched Luminaries, a science conversation series at Boston’s Museum of Science. I joined him onstage, and Rana el Kaliouby moderated. Rana is a pioneer of emotion AI, software that reads human emotion, and the host of the Pioneers of AI podcast. She wrote afterward that she expected Trevor to be witty and funny, but “didn’t expect to be so blown away by his humanity and depth of ideas.”

Here are a few of his insights with his own words highlighted.

When an AI matchmaker Rana built in ChatGPT picked Trevor as her match, he pointed out that it knew very little about either of them. It assembled a plausible answer from what’s on the internet.

Trevor added that when you tell AI it made a mistake, it thanks you but often fails to correct the error: “It’s like a friend who’s been to a lot of therapy but doesn’t actually change.”

When asked how we protect ourselves from AI’s downsides, Trevor said the answer “goes back to something that is very un-technological and very un-AI.” He cited Robert Putnam’s book Bowling Alone, noting that places where communities form accrue many surprising benefits including more accountable governments.

I pushed back that communitarianism, the 1990s movement my father helped found to foster communities, had failed. Trevor responded that we hand too many ideas to intellectuals, who then “apply too much academia” to them. Communitarianism failed, he deadpanned, “because it’s called communitarianism.” An overly academic name.

He noted that nobody calls a phone a failure when the first version doesn’t sell; companies keep re-releasing it. He vowed never to stop investing in community.

Despite his concerns, Trevor has “yet to see a technology that blew up and then left everyone behind.” Cars, computers and the internet all spread to ordinary people.

AI has reached what he calls “work intelligence”: it can do the jobs we invented, but we keep inventing new ones. Salt and ice used to be precious. Now restaurants hand them out for free. What we value changes, and in Trevor’s view, we’re expendable only if we define being human by the tasks we value today.

Our conversation turned to AI’s impact on jobs.

Touring as a comic, Trevor saw towns hollowed out after Kodak and the automaker Studebaker left. Factory workers were told automation was progress. “White-collar workers are now experiencing what many blue-collar workers experienced for decades,” he said. The difference, he argued, is that white-collar workers are closer to power, so newspapers are covering it.

Trevor is confident new jobs will come, as they did after telephone exchange operators disappeared. What worries him is the gap. His analogy is the highway, where the following distance is the space that lets you stop before you hit the car ahead:

Trevor tells tech leaders that “it’s easier to be patient when you are in a position of privilege,” and added, “But ironically, they don’t have patience when it comes to quarterly earnings.”

After ChatGPT took off, show hosts kept telling him weak jokes that ChatGPT had written in a pale imitation of Trevor’s style. He rattled off four reasons AI struggles with humor: there isn’t enough comedy data, the model is a frozen snapshot while what society finds acceptable keeps shifting, comedy depends on knowing your audience (there are jokes you know are funny but you wouldn’t tell your mom), and companies have made models risk averse.

In addition to being the former host of The Daily Show, an award-winning author and a sought-after comedian, Trevor Noah is Microsoft’s Chief Questions Officer.

I reminded him of Picasso’s famous verdict on computers, “They are useless. They can only give you answers,” and joked that as Chief Questions Officer he has something rare these days: job security. He chuckled. Of course, his real job security comes from his depth and humanity, which feed his exceptional humor and wit.

Rana noted that everybody’s getting replaced by AI, but Trevor had played an AI, voicing Griot in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.

He quipped: “Yeah, I’m coming for AI’s job.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5420. Residents Make Big Decisions About Local Businesses Within 30 Days of Moving In. Here’s How One Campaign Used That Window to Fill a Slow Monday Night.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

On a rainy Monday, a Manhattan restaurant landed 50 diners by reaching people who lived just a few blocks away. The exec behind the campaign explains why new neighbors are ready to pick their go-to spots.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A campaign targeting nearby residents brought 50 diners to a restaurant in Manhattan’s Meatpacking District on a rainy Monday night, says.

For Sam Bakhshandehpour, president of local merchants at Bilt, the evening illustrated an opportunity for restaurants facing rising costs and pressure to fill seats.

“No one’s traveling on a Monday night to go grab a meal,” he says.

Rather than trying to attract diners from across the city, Bilt targeted residents in nearby apartment buildings who wouldn’t have to travel far for dinner. The restaurant’s chef-founder was pleased with the results.

“We got 50 covers locally, came on a Monday night where it would’ve been a disaster of a night,” Bakhshandehpour recalls the founder saying.

The guests also spent more, on average, and joined the restaurant’s loyalty program, Bakhshandehpour says.

Bakhshandehpour spent six years helping lead José Andrés Group, most recently as CEO, before moving to Bilt. Years of running hospitality businesses had given him plenty of problems he wanted to solve.

“The costs are going higher, and our margins are getting squeezed every single day,” he says.

When Bilt founder Ankur Jain asked what restaurateurs needed help with, Bakhshandehpour answered, “How much time do you have?”

Bilt began by allowing residents to earn rewards on rent payments. That housing network created an opportunity to connect local businesses with the people moving into nearby homes. Bakhshandehpour says residents make important decisions within their first 30 days in a neighborhood.

“This is my dry cleaner. This is my pharmacy. This is my restaurant, my bar,” he says. “And they’re loyal to their local neighborhood.”

Restaurants once sought those introductions through flyers and menus slipped under apartment doors.

“That’s been digitized,” Bakhshandehpour says. “And that has been localized and personalized to you.”

On that rainy Monday, the campaign gave nearby residents a reason to try the restaurant. Their first visit gave the team a chance to earn the next one.

A restaurant sends something to a table as a complimentary gesture. Then the guest finds it on the bill.

“I didn’t order this, and now you charged me for it,” Bakhshandehpour says.

“Thanks for that level of hospitality,” he adds sarcastically.

The restaurant intended to do something thoughtful. A missed instruction turned it into an awkward conversation.

Bakhshandehpour knows how many details restaurant teams have to carry from one person to another. A reservation request arrives by text. Someone needs to respond, pass it along and make sure the team is ready when the guest walks in.

Technology should help those details reach the people responsible for them.

“You’re able to focus on what you do best, and that’s deliver hospitality to your guests, not worry about the reservation book,” he says.

But every new tool can create another responsibility. As Bilt developed its use of AI agents, Jain set an expectation that Bakhshandehpour remembers clearly.

An operator should be able to ask, “Who’s coming to my restaurant tonight?” in everyday language. Getting an answer shouldn’t require learning how the technology behind it works.

Bakhshandehpour sees that simplicity in a device his father already uses.

“My 84-year-old father sets up his iPhone in a matter of minutes,” he says. “It’s effortless.”

Restaurants also have existing systems they depend on. When I asked whether operators using Toast could connect to Bilt without replacing their point-of-sale platform, Bakhshandehpour said they could.

“We can integrate, you keep Toast,” he says.

To hear where the experience needs work, Bilt sends executives to different cities each quarter for gatherings called Close Friends. Members are invited to give candid feedback.

“They’re the ones who challenge us, they give us the straight talk,” Bakhshandehpour says.

For restaurant teams, the value comes through in the follow-through. The reservation is ready. The instructions reach the right employee. A dish sent as a gift arrives without a charge.

#5419. From paper routes to fighter jets: Shield AI’s bet on Seattle is a homecoming for its co-founders

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 9, 2026 at 6:36 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:36 am

As a kid on Mercer Island, Brandon Tseng delivered The Seattle Times and the Mercer Island Reporter for extra cash. Now he and his older brother, Ryan Tseng, are making news of their own in the Seattle region.

Shield AI, the San Diego defense tech company the brothers co-founded in 2015, announced a deal last week to buy Kirkland, Wash.-based radar maker Echodyne for up to $5.3 billion. Shield, now valued at $28.8 billion, had already unveiled plans in September to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet at a factory south of Seattle.

“I believe we will become one of the largest, or at least the fastest-growing employer in this region over the next several years,” Brandon Tseng said in an interview with GeekWire in the hours after the Echodyne acquisition was announced.

The company projects that it will employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle area by the early 2030s. It estimates the X-BAT could support about 8,000 jobs across the region in all, including jobs at Shield and its suppliers, according to an economic analysis drawing on company figures.

Tseng said Shield expects to have “well north of a million square feet” in the area before long, up from its initial 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash.

“That will really just be the beginning,” he said.

Brandon Tseng said the biggest reason Shield chose the Pacific Northwest for X-BAT production was the region’s “density of engineering and manufacturing talent,” pointing to Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon.

Inside the Echodyne deal: Shield believes the defense tech companies that succeed will need products that “sense, think, and act,” Tseng said. Its Hivemind autonomy software handles the thinking, and its V-BAT drone and X-BAT jet will handle the acting.

Echodyne becomes “the cornerstone of the sensing piece,” he said.

Tseng said Shield got a closer look at the market for sensors when it bought Australian optics company Sentient Vision Systems in 2024. That led the company to start looking seriously at other sensor makers, and eventually to Echodyne.

Shield and Echodyne had first crossed paths in 2016, when both were fledgling companies in the Department of Homeland Security’s Silicon Valley Innovation Program.

Nearly a decade later, the two companies’ teams were talking about working together when Echodyne began exploring a sale, Tseng said. The deal came together over several months. Tseng was at Echodyne the day it was announced last week, as the companies held all-hands meetings with their teams.

It’s an unusual deal: one venture-backed startup buying another, funded in part by a new venture round. Shield is raising $2.5 billion to help pay for the deal, including $1 billion in new funding at the $28.8 billion valuation — more than double what it was worth in March.

Echodyne has about 400 employees, after opening a $40 million radar factory in Woodinville in July. No layoffs are planned, the companies said. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will stay in that role, reporting to Shield CEO Gary Steele. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees.

The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. Tseng said Shield plans a light touch for roughly the first year after that. Echodyne will keep selling radar to other manufacturers, many of them in counter-drone systems, while pursuing performance targets that could add $500 million to the price.

Deeper product integrations will be announced later, he said.

“They’ve been on a tear growth-wise, and we don’t want to get in their way,” Tseng said. “We don’t want to slow them down. We just want to supercharge them.”

He called the two companies’ cultures a strong match, describing both as mission-oriented and engineering-first. Echodyne’s best-selling radar, EchoShield, is designed to protect U.S. and allied service members from incoming drones.

Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders.

Tim Porter, the Madrona Venture Group managing director who has served on Echodyne’s board since 2014, called the deal another sign of the defense tech industry’s rapid growth in the Pacific Northwest.

Echodyne “rarely, if ever, showed up on lists of the hottest defense tech companies,” he wrote. Now it’s “under the radar no longer.”

X-BAT bet: Much of Shield’s growth in the region depends on an aircraft that hasn’t flown yet. Shield unveiled its first full-scale X-BAT prototype this month and shipped it to Kansas for flight testing, with first flight targeted by the end of the year. Shield has said low-rate production will start in Des Moines in mid-2027, with the first locally built jet due in early 2028.

The Pentagon and Shield have committed a combined $400 million to X-BAT’s development, but Shield hasn’t announced any production orders.

Ryan Tseng, speaking to Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference in Munich last week, said Shield expects to announce European X-BAT orders and partnerships but declined to discuss quantities, saying only, “Watch this space.” Andrew Hawkes, Shield’s X-BAT director for Europe, told Breaking Defense the company has “several active” sales campaigns there but declined to name customers.

Asked about the X-BAT schedule in the interview last week, Brandon Tseng acknowledged the challenge but pointed to the engineering and manufacturing teams that brought the prototype together in about a year. “There was no quit in them,” he said.

“It’s hard as hell, right? Just to move out on production that fast, but you have to be confident,” he said. “I’m confident.”

Tseng, a Naval Academy graduate who deployed twice to Afghanistan as a Navy SEAL, compared Shield’s pace to that experience, when small, mission-driven groups with the right tools and resources would “do things that people didn’t think were possible.”

Ryan Tseng, an electrical engineer, previously founded wireless charging company WiPower, which was acquired by Qualcomm. The brothers started Shield with Andrew Reiter, Shield’s first CTO, who returned to the company this year.

Seattle roots: The Tseng brothers and their sister grew up on Mercer Island. Brandon Tseng spent summers swimming in Lake Washington and played water polo for Mercer Island. Ryan Tseng, who was Shield’s CEO for about a decade, graduated from Mercer Island High School, and their sister graduated from the University of Washington.

Their father, Carlos Tseng, was CEO of Seattle-based Foss Maritime from 1996 to 2001, according to Tseng and Shield. He would stop at Pike Place Market on the way home from work, and the family “probably ate salmon every other day,” Brandon Tseng said.

The family moved to Florida in 2001. None of the Tsengs live in the area anymore, but Brandon Tseng still has friends here from middle school and high school and stops by Mercer Island when he has time on his visits to the region.

Shield’s Washington state connections go further. Steele, the company’s CEO since May 2025, grew up in Yakima and graduated from Washington State University.

Brandon Tseng called Shield’s expansion in the region “a fun homecoming” for him, his brother and Steele. He is based in Washington, D.C., but expects to spend more and more time in the Seattle area.

Tseng delivered the Times, then the afternoon paper, seven days a week from age 10 to 14, making his rounds every day after school and on weekends. He credits those routes with teaching him about hard work.

“It’s always felt like home,” he said. “It’s great to be back here.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5418. What a Billion-Dollar Shipwreck Can Teach You About Relentlessly Chasing Your Big Idea

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Bestselling author Julian Sancton dives into his new book, “Neptune’s Fortune,” the story of a legendary sunken treasure, the man who found it and what entrepreneurs can learn from his tireless quest.

Every entrepreneur knows what it means to chase something nobody else can see yet — there’s self-doubt, exhaustion, and long stretches where the only result you’re seeing is money going out the door. But still, you press on.

That pursuit is at the heart of Neptune’s Fortune: The Billion-Dollar Shipwreck and the Ghosts of the Spanish Empire, historian Julian Sancton’s account of one man’s relentless hunt for a legendary sunken Spanish galleon.

The book, named one of Barnes & Noble’s Best Books of 2026, tells the story of the San José, a Spanish galleon loaded with gold and silver that sank off the coast of Colombia in 1708 during a battle with a British squadron. Centuries later, Roger Dooley, a mostly self-taught underwater archaeologist born in New Jersey and raised in Cuba, dove deeply into Spanish archives, found maps that pointed where nobody else was looking, rounded up his own investors and, in 2015, located the wreck 2,000 feet below the surface. His reward? Getting left out of Colombia’s national celebration and an avalanche of lawsuits that have stalled efforts to raise the ship.

This incredible adventure story, Sancton’s follow-up to his New York Times bestselling book Madhouse at the End of the Earth, is a must-read for anyone who has chased a big idea and refused to take no for an answer. I spoke with the author about the book and the countless hours of work that went into writing it, which, as it turns out, has a lot in common with treasure hunting. Here are some highlights of our conversation, edited for length.

Writing a book like this takes years and untold hours of research. Where did it all start?After Madhouse at the End of the Earth, I was looking for my second book, and I didn’t want to be pigeonholed as a writer of harrowing nautical stories. But there was one story that would not let me go. I remembered this almost fairy-tale-like headline about a sunken galleon containing billions of dollars’ worth of gold and silver. But I really didn’t know the story yet. I had no expertise.

So I got it commissioned as an article with my former employer, Vanity Fair. I had another story I was working on at the same time, and I kind of A/B tested it. I’m speaking to Entrepreneur now, so that’s a close analogy to how you road test two products and realize which one is more viable. In writing that article, I discovered my main character, Roger Dooley, who I had really no idea about when I started reporting. People were trying to present him as the villain. And I realized that, no, he was far, far from the villain. He was the person without whom we would not be discussing the San José. I knew that the article just skimmed the surface, and went ahead with the book.

Dan Bova: You describe a scene where Dooley is looking for clues to the sunken ship’s location in an archive that has no discernible organization, and he stumbles onto a map with markings that tell him, “It’s here!” As a historian, do you have those moments? Julian Sancton: Absolutely. I spend a lot of time diving into archives without really knowing what I’m going to find in there — those archives are the equivalent of an ocean for me. And when you find something that can make the facts come alive, those are nuggets of gold. With Madhouse, one of the characters who dies early on is this Norwegian deckhand. While talking to archivists who talk to other archivists, his diary popped up. And it gave all kinds of details and poignant observations about life on that boat. Those finds are the equivalent of Roger Dooley chancing on this critical map, which led him to shift his search area to an area that nobody else was looking at.

Dooley pitched the search for the San José to financial backers and government officials, got yeses, then things fell apart, and he had to start over again. Multiple times. Did that teach you anything?Well, perseverance. Push, push, push. He is absolutely relentless, even now in his 80s. Since the book was published, he’s been giving me advice on how to promote it. He’s saying, “You need to get it in this store and that hand. I went to the Barnes & Noble the other day — it wasn’t even there. You gotta talk to them!” And by the way, I’m proud to inform you that Barnes & Noble selected the book as one of their best books of 2026, so maybe Roger’s sending good vibes out there.

While examining the sea floor, I loved the mindset about why it was good not to find anything. Can you explain that way of thinking?They broke Roger’s search area into sections that could be surveyed using a tried-and-true technique of all surveyors and treasure hunters, which is called “mowing the lawn.” It involves methodically going over an area strip by strip.

By the end of the spring, they hadn’t found anything, and the Colombian authorities were starting to get impatient. But one of his investors, who you would have expected would be upset by this news, was not upset at all. He said something cryptic like, “The remaining 50% is 100%.”

The idea is that when you’re surveying an area, not finding something is determining where it isn’t, and that is very helpful, because it reduces the amount to be searched. But that implies that your research is correct. Not finding something sometimes just also means not finding it.

At Entrepreneur, we talk a lot about imposter syndrome. Dooley seems like the polar opposite. This man was utterly convinced he was the man for the mission, despite not having “official” qualifications and training. What lessons did you learn from him?Dooley believes very much that he has a seat at the table. He never thinks that he’s an imposter, even though many people think that he is. He’s kind of a fake it till you make it guy. In Cuba, he invented the field of maritime archaeology. Did not wait to have a degree in it. He created his own course of study. Because nobody else was cataloging the wrecks around Cuba, he started doing it himself, and then he became the de facto authority.

As eccentric as he is, his drive and his motivation are infectious. He learned valuable lessons working in the film industry in Cuba, and he understood the value of showmanship and presentation and narrative. He created these amazing presentations. He understands the value of a colorful, exciting deck, and that is probably more effective than some exhaustively researched survey.

As you said before, Dooley has been villainized as a “treasure hunter,” which I never really thought of as a derogatory term.I think it’s easy to villainize treasure hunters. But I think their entrepreneurial spirit is actually quite admirable. Treasure hunters like Mel Fisher, Kip Wagner, or Bert Webber embody a kind of quintessential American entrepreneurship. It’s literal venture capitalism. You’re out there taking a massive risk. Frequently, you’re not the one putting down the money, but you’re convincing capitalists of the value of what you’re doing. They’re investing not just because they’re gonna get a huge return on investment if they find something, but because they wanna be involved in something grand. And I think if it weren’t for the adventurism of treasure hunters, a lot of these wouldn’t be found at all.

Legal battles continue over ownership of the shipwreck and its treasure. What do you think would be the fairest outcome?I am in the position of having no horse in the race and just observing this as a writer, as ultimately a romantic. But what I would like to see happen is some kind of international collaboration between the stakeholders in Spain, in Colombia, in the UK. I would love to see a rigorous academic excavation and some kind of museum that would involve Roger as a principal architect. He deserves that not only because of his past accomplishments, but because he knows more about the San José than anybody on earth.

And for the treasure, I mean not just the gold and silver and emeralds, but all the contents — this should be preserved and available for study and admiration for the public and academia. There is no other Spanish galleon from this era that has been rigorously and ethically excavated.

We both live in Westchester. Say you’re kayaking around the Long Island Sound and you tip over and you hit your head on a sunken treasure. Do you report it?Of course!… Well, how big is this treasure? [Laughs]

Every entrepreneur knows what it means to chase something nobody else can see yet — there’s self-doubt, exhaustion, and long stretches where the only result you’re seeing is money going out the door. But still, you press on.

That pursuit is at the heart of Neptune’s Fortune: The Billion-Dollar Shipwreck and the Ghosts of the Spanish Empire, historian Julian Sancton’s account of one man’s relentless hunt for a legendary sunken Spanish galleon.

The book, named one of Barnes & Noble’s Best Books of 2026, tells the story of the San José, a Spanish galleon loaded with gold and silver that sank off the coast of Colombia in 1708 during a battle with a British squadron. Centuries later, Roger Dooley, a mostly self-taught underwater archaeologist born in New Jersey and raised in Cuba, dove deeply into Spanish archives, found maps that pointed where nobody else was looking, rounded up his own investors and, in 2015, located the wreck 2,000 feet below the surface. His reward? Getting left out of Colombia’s national celebration and an avalanche of lawsuits that have stalled efforts to raise the ship.

#5417. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5416. Why This CEO Rebuilt His Best-Selling Product Before Taking It to Target

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Jeff Byers already had one of the best creatines on the market. He raised the bar anyway, then took it to Target

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For years, anyone who asked me about creatine got the same answer. Buy Creapure or Creavitalis and skip everything else. I take creatine every day. I’ve written about why you might want to as well, and I’ve worked in this industry long enough to know how often a label and a scoop disagree.

So when Jeff Byers told me Momentous had moved on from Creapure, I wanted to know why.

“Creapure is amazing,” the co-founder and CEO said, and he was quick to give it credit for the role it played in building Momentous. The change came from what the company calls The Momentous Standard: keep raising your own bar, even when you’re already at the top of the category. “We believed better can be done,” Byers said. That belief is what led to Signature Spec.

I helped launch Momentous more than five years ago, and I wrote about Byers last year when he had just pulled a product bringing in $500,000 a month because the science no longer held up. He has a habit of making expensive decisions. This one may be his biggest, because he made it in the same year he took the brand into Target.

That combination is why I think every founder building a trust-based brand should pay attention. Mass retail has a way of wearing premium brands down. Margins tighten, formulas get cheaper and the marketing gets louder than the product. Momentous is trying to scale without any of that happening. I’ve watched it from the inside, and the company’s approach deserves a close look.

Creatine is one of the most studied supplements on the shelf, backed by more than 685 human clinical trials across ages, doses and durations of up to 14 years. Once a category’s science is settled, most brands compete on format, flavor and price. That’s how we ended up with creatine gummies, and with independent testing that found three of five popular gummies failed, one with less than 25% of the creatine on its label.

Byers went the other direction. “Innovation is quality. Innovation is sourcing,” he told me.

His team found a new manufacturer and wrote its own specification. The result, Signature Spec Creatine, is made in a facility to a 99.99% purity standard, with strict limits on heavy metals. It’s purified with reverse osmosis water filtration in place of the chemical wash common across the industry. It’s also screened for PFAS and microplastics, which standard certifications don’t require. Every batch moves through six stages of testing across four independent groups: Eurofins, Light Labs, NSF Certified for Sport and SuppCo.

As someone who takes creatine daily, I care about those contaminant limits. Anything you take every day for years deserves a higher bar than something you take once.

As a marketer, the line that stuck with me was about the business. Owning the spec, Byers said, “created a robustness in our business that we hadn’t had.” Buying a great branded ingredient means sharing control of quality and supply with a partner. Owning the spec puts both in your hands.

My advice to founders: If your product looks like a commodity on paper, look at the parts customers never see. Sourcing, testing and process take years and real money to build, which is exactly what makes them hard to copy. Investors should be looking there too.

Momentous landed on end caps in nearly 600 Target stores this summer, ahead of a rollout to every store in October. That came months after it entered more than 600 The Vitamin Shoppe locations. The timing lines up with Target’s own plans to grow its wellness assortment by 30% in 2026.

What struck me is how clearly Byers defines each retailer’s role. The Vitamin Shoppe carries 20 to 25 Momentous products and serves as the brand’s home base. “If Momentous had a retail location, it would be The Vitamin Shoppe,” he said. Target carries 12 products and is where new customers discover the brand for the first time.

I asked Byers whether anything changed for Target. The answer was no. The creatine on an end cap comes from the same lots sold to professional and college teams, and everything is still made domestically.

My advice to founders: Before you sign with a big-box retailer, decide what that channel is for. In my work with wellness brands heading into retail, the ones that struggle usually skipped this step and let the retailer decide their assortment for them. A discovery shelf should carry your most essential, easiest-to-understand products. A destination partner can carry the full story. If the margin only works when you water down the formula, the deal is wrong.

When I asked which product might not survive the company’s next science review, Byers said none right now. Then he talked about flavor. The team is moving to real flavors and fewer ingredients, rebuilding its chocolate protein with just cocoa, and leaning on raw ingredients like vanilla bean and cinnamon. Its sleep formula was reformulated with magnesium threonate and now costs less.

The new launches follow the same thinking. Daily Hydration has 100mg of sodium and 50mg of potassium per serving, built for work, travel and light training. Most of us are already getting plenty of sodium, and research using national survey data found 90.7% of U.S. adults exceed the 2,300mg daily limit, while fewer than 2% get the recommended amount of potassium. Many popular electrolyte mixes were built for marathons and then marketed for desk days. Byers calls that overkill for everyday life. Momentous saves the heavier dose for Fuel, its drink for long, intense training.

The brand also recently launched a Pre-Workout powder that lists every ingredient and dose, with no proprietary blends, in a category known for hiding both. It pairs 150mg of caffeine with 300mg of L-theanine, a combination studied for focus without the jitters and it’s become a go-to for me.

Then there’s fiber, the category Byers is most excited about. “Fiber feels like where we were with creatine three or four years ago,” he said. Consumers are thinking about long-term health, and he believes fiber is in its early innings. I agree, and I’d watch this space closely.

My advice to founders: Adding is easy. Cutting takes discipline. Every ingredient you remove is one less thing to source, explain and defend.

In January 2026, Momentous announced a multi-year partnership with Arnold Schwarzenegger. Byers described a three-year process in which Arnold’s team looked at suppliers, manufacturers and track record, and watched the company pull Fadogia and keep reformulating. “This was not about money,” Byers told me. “He would have picked somebody else.”

I’ve spent much of my career building partnerships between brands and the people who represent them. The ones that last look like this. The diligence runs both ways, and the decision rests on years of behavior.

Fast growth is usually where culture breaks, and Byers learned that firsthand. After an earlier merger, he spent six to nine months rebuilding a company that had lost its way.

“Teams ultimately build those standards or kill those standards,” he said. Momentous now has more red tape than ever, and Byers sees his job as protecting the scrappiness that got it here. “Don’t underestimate the values that you put in place.”

Momentous could have kept using one of the best creatines in the world, and no one would have questioned it. Byers and his co-founder, Erica Good, chose to raise their own bar instead, then put the result in front of millions of Target shoppers. Target will test whether Momentous can hold its standards at scale. After five years of watching this team make the expensive call, I’d bet on it.

For years, anyone who asked me about creatine got the same answer. Buy Creapure or Creavitalis and skip everything else. I take creatine every day. I’ve written about why you might want to as well, and I’ve worked in this industry long enough to know how often a label and a scoop disagree.

So when Jeff Byers told me Momentous had moved on from Creapure, I wanted to know why.

“Creapure is amazing,” the co-founder and CEO said, and he was quick to give it credit for the role it played in building Momentous. The change came from what the company calls The Momentous Standard: keep raising your own bar, even when you’re already at the top of the category. “We believed better can be done,” Byers said. That belief is what led to Signature Spec.

#5415. The Best Leaders Never Stop Sharing the Lessons They’ve Learned. Here’s Why It Matters More Than You Think.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Decades of hard-earned business wisdom matters most when leaders are willing to share the full story behind it, not just the outcome.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Over the past few decades, leaders have lived through the Great Recession, Covid and now the rise of artificial intelligence. Each has fundamentally changed how companies operate and how leaders make decisions.

The experience of leaders who lived through those challenges — and how they pivoted in unprecedented times — contains invaluable knowledge. Too often, people think they can recapture history just by reading about it. Learning from history is useful, of course. But leadership experience isn’t something that can be replicated just by asking AI a question. Real people had to navigate real situations to keep their companies afloat, and that can’t be fully understood from the answer to a prompt.

Decades of experience are most valuable when the leaders who lived through it are willing to pass on what they learned. Not just the outcome, but the full story behind it. Here’s why.

No two business decisions are exactly alike. Looking back at what someone did in a similar situation and copying it rarely works, because the decision itself isn’t the defining factor. What mattered was the thinking behind it: the pressures, the constraints, the information available at the time. None of that gets passed down unless the person who lived it chooses to share it.

That’s why sharing the context behind a tough call, and not just the decision itself, is so important. The best leaders explain what led them down a particular path, because that reasoning is important. Without it, people start making decisions by pattern-matching to a single past example, and miss the nuance.

Frameworks offer direction, but direction isn’t the same as confidence. Confidence comes from people who have been there, done that and can give sound advice. Someone who has faced similar challenges can ask the right questions, challenge assumptions and offer a perspective that helps leaders see their decisions more clearly. That insight can give leaders the confidence to move forward.

A leader’s mettle is tested in situations they’ve never seen before and likely never will again. Leaders who share what they’ve learned give the next generation a real place to start instead of a blank page. That’s a completely different kind of value than theory can provide.

Almost every leader who’s achieved something meaningful can point to someone who helped them along the way — a mentor who believed in them, offered guidance or helped them navigate a difficult decision. All those experiences, and all the people who helped you get there, are a gift. And leaders who have benefited from that kind of support often feel a calling to pass it on to others.

It’s why some pursue business coaching as a second career when they are ready to move on from the CEO role. CEOs are builders. While they may be ready to leave the responsibilities of running a company behind, they still want to develop people, solve problems and make a meaningful impact. Looking back over long careers, many CEOs say their greatest successes involved helping others succeed.

There’s another benefit to mentoring that many experienced leaders don’t anticipate: They continue growing themselves. I’ve seen leaders leave the CEO role, begin coaching others and discover they’re developing in ways they never expected. They gain greater empathy for other people and a deeper understanding of the challenges different leaders face. After decades of making decisions and being responsible for outcomes, they find themselves learning just as much from the people they’re helping.

That’s what makes mentoring so rewarding. Mentors are not simply passing along everything they’ve learned over their careers. They’re continuing to grow as leaders and as people.

Effective mentoring means helping people see past their blind spots. Confirmation bias might be the most common one of all. It’s easy to believe an idea and then go find justification that matches it. AI is particularly good at feeding that instinct back, since it tends to reflect whatever perspective it’s given rather than challenge it.

That’s what makes outside perspectives so valuable. Experienced leaders can offer fresh perspectives, challenge assumptions and push leaders to think beyond the answer they’ve already convinced themselves is right.

None of this works if the story that a mentor passes on only includes the good parts. Most of the real wisdom comes from mistakes. When someone is vulnerable enough to admit they messed up, the real learning happens. That’s the full story, not the polished version.

Experience that never gets passed on doesn’t do anyone much good. It stays with the person who earned it. The leaders we remember are the ones who made sure what they learned — wins and losses — outlasted their own careers.

Over the past few decades, leaders have lived through the Great Recession, Covid and now the rise of artificial intelligence. Each has fundamentally changed how companies operate and how leaders make decisions.

The experience of leaders who lived through those challenges — and how they pivoted in unprecedented times — contains invaluable knowledge. But leadership experience isn’t something that can be replicated just by asking AI a question. Real people had to navigate real situations to keep their companies afloat, and that can’t be fully understood from the answer to a prompt.

Decades of experience are most valuable when the leaders who lived through it are willing to pass on what they learned. Not just the outcome, but the full story behind it. Here’s why.
